blocks.text: Wesgro's FY26 to FY30 plan sets six tourism targets, each over the plan's five years (Wesgro, Strategic Plan 2025/26 to 2029/30, p20). Two of them also measure Wesgro's strategic outcomes for leisure tourism and business events: 800,000 to 1 million new international tourist arrivals and 161 business event bids secured, worth an estimated R4.5 billion (Inception Report, Nov 2025, p6). The other four are 250 ship calls, 10 new air routes, three international tourism marketing campaigns and 12,500 international tourism trade engagements. A new route is a scheduled international service flying to and from Cape Town for the first time (Wesgro, Strategic Plan 2025/26 to 2029/30, p59). The table sets each target beside what this report carries.

Add the finding that activity targets hold today's pace while the outcome asks for a step change, and the consideration outcome (assessment 6). The base year of 'new' arrivals stays open (decisions). blocks.text: The five-year period decides how the arrivals target compares with the growth case. From 2025 to 2030 the base case adds about 304,000 arrivals and the accelerated case about 443,000 (Market Assessment Report, May 2026, p19, p20; computed). Wesgro's 800,000 to 1 million is 2.6 to 3.3 times the base case's gain and about twice the accelerated case's (computed). No modelled path delivers it by 2030; the two paths need ten years to add 676,949 and 1,017,453 (Market Assessment Report, May 2026, p19). Wesgro's own target therefore sharpens the case that growth is a supply programme. [Wesgro to confirm the base year from which the new arrivals are counted.]

The activity targets, by contrast, roughly hold today's pace. Each year they ask for about 32 bids, 50 ship calls and two new routes. The recent pace is 36 bids secured and 79 vessels in 2024/25, and about 1.7 new routes a year from 2015 to 2025 (Wesgro, Strategic Plan 2025/26 to 2029/30, p20; Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p36; Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p37; MIDAS Aviation Market Assessment, Mar 2026, "International Comparisons"; computed). The cruise target sits below the last season partly because its base leaves out the ships rerouted in 2023/24. Trade engagements stay at 2,500 a year, flat on FY24. The step change sits in the outcome, not in the activity.

Wesgro calls the outcome behind its arrivals target "growth in leisure tourism consideration in international and local markets" (Inception Report, Nov 2025, p6; Wesgro, Strategic Plan 2025/26 to 2029/30, p19). Yet consideration is not the constraint: about 97 million high-value travellers are interested in South Africa, and about 1.4 million convert (section 1.3). When it next revises its plan, Wesgro should state the outcome as conversion and value.

blocks.text: Growth for Jobs also sets a value test. It calls tourism the province's most obvious service export and aims to triple the value of the province's exports of goods and services, tourism included, by 2035 (Growth for Jobs Strategy 2023, p11, p14). On the model's base case, direct foreign spend rises about 1.5 times from the modelled R27.12bn of 2024 to R40.6bn in 2035, in constant 2024 rand (Market Assessment Report, May 2026, p24; computed). That falls short of the tripling G4J sets for exports as a whole, though the bases differ, so alignment will be tested on value, not only arrivals. Chapter 5 tracks spend, season and spread beside arrivals.

blocks.text: Wesgro's FY26 to FY30 plan is the second test, and its six targets let alignment rest on numbers rather than principle. The timing fits too. Chapter 4 sets its first decision gate at the end of 2028, inside the plan period and before the base case crosses the model's seat line. That gate is the point to map the initiatives' outputs to the plan's six targets and to state which of them the action plan would raise.

The Tourism Blueprint 2030, the province's sector roadmap, is not one of the contract's two tests, but it points the same way. Its objectives include growing visitor numbers and yield, raising the destination's global profile and improving customer experiences. Others are to develop tourism infrastructure, spread tourism benefits geographically, prioritise district tourism development, ease business for tourism firms and build industry partnerships (Tourism Blueprint 2030, p9). These map onto the action plan's three pillars. Numbers, yield and profile sit in demand; infrastructure, spread, district development and customer experience in supply; partnerships and ease of business in enablement. The Blueprint's renewed focus on domestic markets lies outside this study's international mandate.

blocks.text: Cruise calls have grown without new berth capacity. The province hosted 70, 67 and 79 vessels in the 2022/23, 2023/24 and 2024/25 seasons, carrying 144,125, 109,884 and 127,178 passengers (Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p37). International passengers rose from 55,495 to 100,255 over the same seasons, while total passengers fell about 12% (StratEcon, Cruise Liner Economic Contribution Study 2024/25, Oct 2025, p9, p10; Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p37; computed). For 2024/25 the cruise study counts 127,128 passengers, against the Diagnostic's 127,178, and 106,315 unique passengers once double counting is removed, the measure Chapter 5 tracks (StratEcon, Cruise Liner Economic Contribution Study 2024/25, Oct 2025, p8, p9). The Cape Town berth took 83 calls in 2024/25, with 127,000 passengers (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p110). [StratEcon 2024/25 cruise report to confirm whether 79 vessels and 83 calls differ by definition.] That season added R1.79bn to provincial GDP-R after displacement, from about R1.99bn of spend before it, and supported 1,234 direct and 2,345 total jobs in the province (StratEcon, Cruise Liner Economic Contribution Study 2024/25, Oct 2025, p19, p22, p24, p27). Value has come from the international mix, not volume.

blocks.text: Tourism weighs most in the smaller district economies. In 2023 tourist spend equalled 15.6% to 16.8% of GDPR in four outer districts: the West Coast, the Overberg, the Garden Route and the Central Karoo. It equalled 7.0% in the Cape Winelands and 6.7% in the Metro (Municipal Economic Review and Outlook 2024/25, West Coast, p131; Municipal Economic Review and Outlook 2024/25, Overberg, p119; Municipal Economic Review and Outlook 2024/25, Garden Route, p151; Municipal Economic Review and Outlook 2024/25, Central Karoo, p111; Municipal Economic Review and Outlook 2024/25, Cape Winelands, p113; Municipal Economic Review and Outlook 2024/25, Cape Metro, p72). The Metro holds the volume, but a fall in visitors costs the outer districts more of their economy.
